001_1947-06-21_Maury Island, Puget Sound.report_summary:
**Document:** FBI teletype/memo dated **August 14, 1947** from **J. Edgar Hoover** to the Communications Section, **SAC, Seattle** (file code shown as **CC-150**; case-file provenance from **62-HQ-83894, Section 2**). The memo responds to a prior telegram (“REURTEL AUGUST TWELVE”) and directs Seattle to reinterview the principals. It is administrative/investigative in nature rather than a fresh field observation report.

**Witness:** The underlying claim centers on **Harold Dahl**, a civilian boat operator, and **Fred Crisman**. The memo also references **Emil Smith** as an interview source, plus “Arnold” in connection with anonymous calls. The report treats Dahl and Crisman as the original storytellers and the key witnesses whose statements were being tested.

**Sighting:** This is the well-known **Maury Island** flying-disc/fragments incident in the **Tacoma / Puget Sound** area. The original alleged event was the discovery and recovery of metal fragments said to be from a flying disc, with the claim later discussed at a conference on **July 31, 1947** and a supposed admission that the story was a hoax on **Saturday night, August 2, 1947**.

**Object:** The alleged object was not a full craft but **“material”/fragments** claimed to be debris from a flying disc. The memo says the story had been repeated to Army intelligence officers and that the fragments were allegedly taken on a fatal flight by **Captain Davidson** and **Lieutenant Brown**.

**Investigation:** Hoover states that, if Emil Smith’s account is correct, Dahl and Crisman had repeated the false story until Dahl admitted it was a hoax. The memo concludes that either Smith or Arnold may have made the anonymous phone calls under the belief the material was real, but that the matter should be cleared up by **reinterviewing Dahl and Crisman**. Once clarified, Hoover says, **no further investigation is necessary**. The document strongly frames the incident as a **hoax**, not a validated UFO sighting.
001_1947-06-21_Maury Island, Puget Sound.report_summary_zh:

**Witness:** 其核心主张围绕**Harold Dahl**——一名平民船只操作员——以及**Fred Crisman**。备忘录还提及**Emil Smith**作为一名访谈来源，并在匿名来电的相关内容中提到“Arnold”。报告将Dahl和Crisman视为最初讲述故事的人，也是其陈述正被核实的关键证人。

**Sighting:** 这就是众所周知的**Maury Island**飞碟/碎片事件，发生在**Tacoma / Puget Sound**地区。最初所谓的事件是发现并回收金属碎片，据称这些碎片来自一架飞碟；后来在**July 31, 1947**的一次会议上再次讨论该说法，并据称在**Saturday night, August 2, 1947**承认这一故事是骗局。

001_1947-07-26_Saybrook, Illinois (front.report_summary:
**Document:** FBI Office Memorandum, Standard Form No. 64, from the SAC, Springfield, to the Director, FBI, dated August 20, 1947. The memo references Bureau Bulletin No. 42 (Series 1947), dated July 30, 1947, and carries internal file markings for FBI case 62-0-1445 / SI File 62-0-1445. The second page is the enclosure cover sheet: “Photographs of ‘Flying Disc’ found at Saybrook, Ill. 7-26-47,” indicating six photos enclosed.

**Witness:** Mrs. June Anderson of Saybrook, Illinois, reported the discovery to the Springfield FBI office. The memo gives no indication that she was a trained observer; instead, an agent’s follow-up inquiry notes that her “stability” was questionable, suggesting the reporting circumstances were somewhat unreliable or at least informal.

**Sighting:** The reported event occurred at about 6:00 A.M. on July 26, 1947, when Mrs. Anderson found a “flying disc” in her front yard. The enclosure and memo identify the location only as Saybrook, Illinois.

**Object:** The object was not an aerial craft. Investigation found it to be an old wooden platter with a silver plate, a spark plug, a timer, and pieces of old brass tubing attached. The agent concluded it was apparently assembled from parts gathered by juveniles in the area. The memo explicitly states, “No doubt this was someone’s idea of a prank.”

**Investigation:** Springfield retained the disc pending Bureau guidance, noting that Washington might want to examine it for any novel value. Six photographs were taken and enclosed. The report is therefore best understood as a prank-object recovery case rather than a genuine UFO encounter, despite the contemporary “flying disc” terminology.

The memo also references Mr. and Mrs. Gaylon Caldwell, Mr. and Mrs. Fred Thunell, Mr. and Mrs. Norman Hall, Keith Hughes, Joan Crookston, and others. Some names appeared in a newspaper account but later denied observing the objects because they had not had the opportunity; this suggests the local press report was at least partly inaccurate.

**Sighting:** The sightings occurred in Logan, Utah, on the evening of September 8, 1947, mainly between about 10:30 and 11:10 p.m. One account said approximately a dozen objects moved in group formation at 2,000-3,000 feet, were small like pigeons, white and illuminated, showed no wing movement, and disappeared to the north after circling the city for about 1-2 minutes. Rainier, Arnold reports climbing to roughly 9,500 feet and crossing the southwest side of the mountain. 001_1947-07-29_Oakland, California (seen.report_summary:
**Document:** Confidential memorandum for the Officer in Charge, Incident 4AF 1208-I, dated 5 August 1947. The report was prepared by James A. Nelson, Special Agent, CIC 4AF, from an interview with Captain William H. Ryherd at the 415th AAF BU, Building 95, Hamilton Field, California. The page is marked confidential and later declassified under NND 90986.

**Witness:** Primary witness was Capt. William H. Ryherd (ASN O-66356), assistant operations officer in the 415th AAF BU and instructor pilot in the 415th Training Unit. He was accompanied by student 1st Lt. Ward L. Stewart during the sighting.

**Sighting:** On 29 July 1947 at about 1450, after landing an AT-6 near the hangar at Hamilton Field, Ryherd looked west over the hangar and saw a P-80 flying southward toward Oakland. Above the P-80, at roughly 8,000 to 10,000 feet, he observed two flying objects moving in the same direction. He estimated them at about 15 to 25 feet in diameter and described them as solid, white, somewhat shiny, and circular, “like a ball on the bottom, but not completely round.” He specifically said they were not airplanes.

**Object:** The first object moved straight and level; the second followed close behind at the same altitude, alternating left-to-right and right-to-left in a way that resembled an aircraft in formation. Ryherd said their speed made the P-80 appear motionless by comparison. The sky was clear, and the objects disappeared in flight, supposedly over Oakland, heading toward the ocean.

**Investigation:** No sound was heard, though the P-80’s noise may have masked it. Ryherd reported no vapor, smoke, or visible trail. He also said he had told no one before because he feared people would think he was crazy. The agent’s note states Ryherd showed extreme sincerity and answered questions with caution and assurance.

**Sighting:** 1947年7月29日约 1450 时，Ryherd 在 Hamilton Field（汉密尔顿机场）机库附近降落一架 AT-6 后，向西越过机库张望，看见一架 P-80 正向南飞往 Oakland（奥克兰）。在 P-80 上方，约 8,000 to 10,000 英尺高度处，他观察到两个飞行物体朝同一方向移动。他估计这两个物体直径约 15 to 25 英尺，并描述它们为实心、白色、略带光泽、呈圆形，“像一个底部是球形的东西，但又不完全是圆的。”他明确表示它们不是飞机。

001_1947-06-02_Rehoboth Beach, Sussex Co.report_summary:
**Document:** Newspaper clipping attached to an FBI Baltimore routing sheet in case file 62-HQ-83894, Section 2, subject line "FLYING DISCS / MISCELLANEOUS," dated 9/4/47. The clipping is a contemporary press account rather than a Bureau investigative narrative, but it was preserved in the flying-disc file as corroborating correspondence/report material.

**Witness:** Forrest Wenyon of 123 Rehoboth Avenue, Rehoboth Beach, was described as a veteran Delaware pilot with about 30 years' flying experience and as the Rehoboth Airport attendant. That background gives the article some credibility as an aviation observer, though the piece is clearly framed as a sensational newspaper story.

**Sighting:** Wenyon said he first noticed a strange object the previous September while flying around 1,000 feet, and then saw another on June 2, 1947 while piloting a Stinson four-passenger aircraft at about 1,400 feet. He described the craft as looking like a "flying mayonnaise jar" or "jar," moving at tremendous speed, crossing his path from west to east, and disappearing after only a few seconds.

He characterized the motion as guided rather than erratic, and suggested a rocket-like or jet-propelled mechanism. He later speculated that one of these objects might have been involved in the Eastern Airlines crash at Port Deposit, Maryland, on Memorial Day.

**Investigation:** The clipping says Wenyon contacted the Federal Bureau of Investigation, Eastern Airlines, and the Civil Aeronautics Authority, but received no answer. The article embeds his report within a broader roundup of flying-saucer claims nationwide, including references to Harvard Observatory and Army/Navy interest, but it does not record any official identification or Bureau conclusion.
001_1947-06-02_Rehoboth Beach, Sussex Co.report_summary_zh:
**Document:** 附在 62-HQ-83894 案卷第 2 部分中一份 FBI Baltimore routing sheet（巴尔的摩流转单）上的报纸剪报，主题行写着“FLYING DISCS / MISCELLANEOUS”，日期为 9/4/47。该剪报是当时的新闻报道，而非局方的调查叙述，但作为佐证信函/报告材料，被保存在飞碟档案中。

**Witness:** 来自 123 Rehoboth Avenue, Rehoboth Beach 的 Forrest Wenyon 被描述为一名有约 30 年飞行经验的特拉华州资深飞行员，同时也是 Rehoboth Airport 的值班人员。这样的背景使这篇文章作为航空观察者的陈述具有一定可信度，不过该报道显然是以耸动性的报纸故事方式写成的。

**Sighting:** Wenyon 说，他第一次注意到一个奇怪物体是在前一年的 9 月，当时他正以约 1,000 feet 的高度飞行；随后他又在 1947 年 6 月 2 日看到另一个物体，当时他正驾驶一架 Stinson 四座飞机，飞行高度约 1,400 feet。他形容该飞行器看起来像一个“flying mayonnaise jar”或“jar”，以极快速度移动，从西向东穿过他的航线，仅几秒钟后便消失了。

**Object:** 文章称，Wenyon 观察到尾部有银色火焰，他认为那是推进装置；尾部看起来还像一个带有孔洞的盖子，火焰便从这些孔中喷出。他将其运动特征描述为受控而非无规则，并推测其可能是类似火箭或喷气推进的机制。后来他还猜测，这些物体中的一个可能与 Memorial Day 发生在 Maryland 的 Port Deposit 的 Eastern Airlines 坠机事件有关。

**Investigation:** 这篇剪报称，Wenyon 曾联系 Federal Bureau of Investigation、Eastern Airlines 和 Civil Aeronautics Authority，但未得到任何答复。文章将他的报告嵌入到全国范围内更大的一组飞碟说法综述之中，其中提及了 Harvard Observatory 以及 Army/Navy 的兴趣，但未记录任何官方认定或局方结论。

001_1947-07-04_Lake St. Clair area (near.report_summary:
**Document:** This is a single handwritten incoming letter page in FBI case file 62-HQ-83894 (Section 1), stamped with a "G.I.R." mark and an instruction to "KEEP ENVELOPE ATTACHED" / "Anonymous notification," indicating the Bureau wanted the original envelope preserved. No separate continuation page is visible here, and the page appears to be a self-contained report fragment rather than part of a longer multi-page narrative.

**Witness:** The writer is not identified on the visible page. The text is addressed "Dear Mr. ..." and reads like a personal communication to an official or correspondent rather than a formal field report. Because no signature, rank, or occupation is visible, the witness should be treated as an unnamed civilian observer.

**Sighting:** The witness says they "have also seen a flying saucer" on the evening of July 4 at about 10:30 p.m., while sitting on a porch. The object was reportedly "in the air at the same level" as two obvious portions of light in the searchlight beams coming from an air field near Lake St. Clair. The witness notes that there were two clearly outlined beams, with one partly faded, and that the lights/object appeared aligned with the beam level.

**Object:** The description is limited and impressionistic: no definite shape, size, speed, color, or maneuvering is provided beyond the comparison to the searchlight beams. The writer immediately offers a skeptical interpretation, saying that a few trucks with proper equipment could create the same illusion. That comment suggests the observer believed the phenomenon may have been an optical effect or a misread light source rather than a structured craft.

**Investigation:** The page has the hallmarks of FBI file handling rather than an Air Force technical report: administrative stamps, envelope-retention instructions, and a fragmentary civilian narrative. Based on the witness's own wording, the best analytical conclusion is that this is a probable light/beam illusion near a local airfield around Lake St. Clair, not a well-documented aircraft or disc encounter.
001_1947-07-04_Lake St. Clair area (near.report_summary_zh:

**Sighting:** 目击者称自己在 7 月 4 日晚上约 10:30 坐在门廊上时，“也看见了一个飞碟”。据称该物体“在空中，位于同一高度”，对应于来自 Lake St. Clair 附近一处机场的探照灯光束中两个明显光段的位置。目击者指出，有两道轮廓清晰的光束，其中一道部分变淡，而这些灯光/物体看上去与光束高度齐平。

**Investigation:** 这页具有典型的 FBI 案卷处理特征，而非 USAF 的技术报告特征：有行政盖章、保留信封的指示，以及一段零散的平民叙述。根据目击者自身的措辞，最合理的分析结论是：这大概是 Lake St. Clair 附近一处本地机场上空的光束/灯光幻象，而非一次有充分记录的飞机或飞碟遭遇。

001_1947-07-04_Omaha, Nebraska, USA_65_h.report_summary:
**Document:** Handwritten one-page correspondence in FBI file 62-HQ-83894 (Section 1), page p.0014. The page is signed by Fred R. Reibold and gives his address as 2315 Rinehart Ave., Omaha, Nebraska. No page-2 marker or continuation page is present, so this page stands alone as the complete event-related document in the set shown.

**Witness:** Fred R. Reibold, a civilian correspondent in Omaha, challenges an earlier explanation reportedly offered by Dr. Kenny. Reibold writes that the material or object in question was "not tobacco ashes" and says the explanation is unsatisfactory and "ridicule." His tone suggests he is a firsthand witness or an informed participant in the underlying incident.

**Sighting:** Reibold states the object/material burned with "such extreme heat" that it scorched pavement on and near the spot where it landed. He adds that it "possibly" could have been a "late Fourth of July firework or something similar," which is the only explicit time clue on the page and supports a July 4, 1947 event.

**Object:** The item is not described as a flying disc or craft on this page; instead it is treated as hot residue or a small object that lit on the pavement and caused scorching. Reibold specifically rejects the idea that it was pipe ash/tobacco ash.

**Investigation:** The page appears to be FBI-file correspondence rather than a formal investigative report, with no visible classification stamp or report number beyond the master file code. The document’s analytical value is limited: the writer disputes the "pipe ashes" explanation and offers a tentative, non-UFO possibility of a late July 4 firework. No definitive conclusion is recorded on the page beyond Reibold’s rejection of the earlier identification.

001_1947-07-06_Darlington, South Carolin.report_summary:
**Document:** This page is a Western Union full-rate telegram addressed to the **US Dept. of Justice, Washington, D.C.** and later stamped/handled by the **FBI**. It appears in the declassified FBI flying-disc correspondence file **62-HQ-83894, Section 1**. The face of the form shows the Western Union service notes and an FBI receipt stamp dated **7 Jul 1947**. No formal classification marking is visible on the page itself.

**Witness:** The sender/signer is **J. U. Watts Jr.** The page does not identify a rank, occupation, or affiliation beyond being the civilian correspondent reporting the event.

**Sighting:** Watts reported that **“about 12 so-called flying discs”** passed over **Darlington, South Carolina** at **approximately 5:30 PM today**. The telegram was filed/transmitted from Darlington at **6:30 PM** and time-stamped by Western Union at **6:50 PM** on **6 Jul 1947**.

**Object:** The message provides only a brief count and the popular label “flying discs.” It does not describe size, color, altitude, direction, speed, formation, sound, or duration beyond the estimate of about twelve objects.

**Investigation:** The telegram asks, **“advise if wish details,”** suggesting a possible follow-up, but this page contains no reply or subsequent analysis. As a stand-alone report, it is an uncorroborated, low-detail civilian sighting with no technical description or immediate explanatory conclusion beyond the sender’s assertion that multiple disc-like objects passed overhead.

No continuation page is present here, so this appears to be a standalone correspondence item.

**Witness:** The writer is not named on the page. The dateline reads "Yoakum, July 12, 1947, 10:20 PM," indicating a civilian correspondent from Yoakum, Texas. Because the author is anonymous and provides no contact details, occupation, or corroborating witnesses, the evidentiary value is limited.

**Sighting:** The letter describes a "flying of fire" or fire-like aerial phenomenon near Yoakum. Although the handwriting is difficult to read, the account suggests a luminous object or effect that "arced around" and caused people to be afraid, with the writer implying it was seen not far from town. The page gives no clear object shape, altitude, duration, direction of travel, or number of witnesses.

**Investigation:** No explicit FBI analysis, identification, or follow-up appears on this page. The report is vague, emotionally phrased, and partly garbled, so it should be treated as an unverified postwar flying-disc-era letter rather than a well-documented sighting. The best reading is of a fire-like light or object reported near Yoakum on the evening of Jul 12, 1947, with the document itself being entered into the FBI files three days later.

001_1947-08-18_Omaha, Douglas County, Ne.report_summary:
**Document:** One-page newspaper clipping pasted to an FBI enclosure sheet in file 62-HQ-83894, Section 1. The page is stamped "ENCLOSURE" and marked in red "62-83894-4"; no FBI narrative text appears on the sheet, only the clipped newspaper article.

**Witness:** The article does not name the person who reported or recovered the alleged object. The only named local source is Dr. C. L. Kenny, head of the chemistry department at the Creighton College of Dentistry, who had two students analyze the material.

**Sighting:** The clipping reports that a supposed "flying saucer" that fell near 2319 Himebaugh Avenue in Omaha on Monday evening was examined and found to be nothing unusual. The residue was described as ashes, and the article gives no true flight details, but instead frames the incident as a local misidentification. Kenny said the sample contained sodium, potassium, iron, aluminum, carbonate, sulphate, and unburnt carbon.

**Investigation:** Kenny concluded the analysis matched ordinary pipe tobacco ash, stating, "This is the same analysis you would get from ordinary pipe tobacco." The headline, "'Flying Saucer' Just Someone's Pipe Dream," signals the article's debunking conclusion. In the context of the 1947 flying-disc wave, the FBI preserved the clipping as correspondence evidence, but this page contains no Bureau investigation, interview notes, or further corroboration beyond the newspaper report.

001_1947-07-06_Wisconsin, USA (Janesvill.report_summary:
**Document:** This page is a newspaper-clipping attachment preserved in FBI file 62-HQ-83894, Section 1 (flying-disc correspondence/reports, 1947). No FBI agent narrative, signature, or case memo appears on the page; instead it contains two Associated Press stories laid out as clipped newsprint.

**Witness:** The local Wisconsin roundup names several civilian observers, led by Dick Thompson of Janesville, who phoned police after seeing the object. Other named witnesses include Mrs. L. A. Davis and her husband near Oshkosh, and Eugene Le Plant and his 12-year-old son Duane near Green Bay.

**Sighting:** Thompson reportedly saw a "flying disk" about 12:15 a.m. Sunday. The Davis family reported a round, silvery object at 6:45 p.m. Sunday while driving six miles west of Oshkosh. In Green Bay, the Le Plants said they watched a rapidly moving silver ball or disk about 6:30 p.m. Wednesday from their garden on the western edge of the city. Descriptions across the article emphasize roundness, speed, altitude, and intermittent visibility; one witness said it first looked like an airplane, then "appeared as big as the sun."

**Object:** The objects were described as disk-shaped, silvery, very fast, and high; one vanished when the witness stopped the car and got out to look again. The headline also notes that a disc reportedly found by a priest was actually a circular saw, underscoring the confusion surrounding the reports.

**Investigation:** The page mixes local reporting with an AP science analysis by Howard W. 001_1947-07-09_North Hollywood, Los Ange.report_summary:
**Document:** FBI Office Memorandum from the SAC, Los Angeles, to the Director, FBI, dated July 17, 1947, in file 62-HQ-83894 Section 1. The first page is a standard Office Memorandum with subject “Recovery of ‘Flying Disc,’ North Hollywood, California, July 9, 1947”; the second page continues the same memo, so both pages belong to one report. The file copy includes recording/indexing marks, enclosure notation for photos, and later file stamps showing the copies were destroyed in 1964.

**Witness/Report Source:** The initial report came from the North Hollywood area after a “flying disc” was said to have landed near Radford and Magnolia Streets. Battalion Fire Chief Wallace E. Newcomb told FBI Agent SA Richard D. Auerbach that, at about 10:30 p.m., an unknown woman telephoned in an excited state and said the disc had dropped into her garden at 11858 Magnolia Boulevard. She was not named in the memo. The next day, civilian Frank V. Brown of 6552 Teesdale Avenue said he heard neighborhood talk at a service station and believed local students may have been involved in making the object.

**Sighting/Recovery:** The object was reportedly on fire when first found and was extinguished by a fire department truck before being taken to the station and then to the FBI office. The scene attracted newspaper reporters and photographers. The memo frames the event as a recovery rather than a prolonged airborne observation.

**Object:** FBI’s description says the device consisted of two convex steel discs about 2 feet in diameter, fused at the outer edge and joined at the center by a hollow cylindrical connection. It had a vertical galvanized iron fin, a short closed pipe projecting inward from the rim, and what appeared to be a radio tube in the center top, weighing about 20 pounds.

**Investigation/Conclusion:** SA Auerbach arranged photos and forwarded them for Bureau inspection. The object was later turned over to Major Courtney W. Hempstead, A.C., G-2, Fort MacArthur, San Pedro, who reported it was definitely a hoax and could not have flown under its own power. The memo’s overall conclusion is that the North Hollywood “flying disc” was fabricated rather than a genuine aerial craft.

001_1947-07-10_Black River Falls, Wiscon.report_summary:
**Document:** This is a Standard Form No. 64 Office Memorandum from D. M. Ladd to Mr. E. A. Tamm, dated July 11, 1947, in FBI file 62-HQ-83894. The page bears later FBI routing/stamp markings, including an EX-56 notation and file handling stamps, showing it was entered into the Bureau’s flying-disc correspondence file. The memo reports secondhand information relayed by the Milwaukee FBI office through SAC Johnson.

**Witness:** The principal named witness is Sig Hanson, identified as the City Engineer at Black River Falls, Wisconsin. His report reached the FBI via Colonel Harry Schafer, a Reserve Officer with the Civilian Air Patrol. Schafer appears to be the immediate source who phoned SAC Johnson; Hanson is the person who allegedly found the object.

**Sighting/Recovery:** At about 3:30 p.m. on July 10, 1947, Hanson reportedly found a large 17-inch disc. The object was described as possibly cardboard painted with silver airplane dope. In the center was a tube and a small motor with a propeller attached to the side. Colonel Schafer expressed the view that the disc would not be able to fly by itself. The memo does not describe anyone seeing the object in flight; it concerns a recovered disc-like item.

**Investigation:** Schafer said the item would be taken to Air Corps Headquarters, but Hanson did not want to release it without FBI approval. Ladd instructed Johnson to tell Schafer the Bureau had no reason to try to secure the material because it was not in FBI custody and the Bureau had no control over it. Ladd also noted that the press was asking about the matter and instructed that no comment be made. Overall, the memorandum treats the item as a likely homemade or non-aerodynamic object rather than a credible flying craft report.

**Witness:** F. C. Hairston of 1554 Texas Avenue, Shreveport, Louisiana. He is identified only as a civilian observer, not as a trained aviation or scientific witness. The report says he notified military personnel at Barksdale Field immediately after recovering the object.

He said it landed in the 1500 block of Texas Avenue, and that he picked it up at 1554 Texas Avenue. He described the object as whirling in flight, with fire “spouting from sides.” The fire stopped on landing, and smoke appeared a few seconds later. He stated the disc was not hot when recovered.

**Object:** The FBI teletype describes a thin aluminum disc about 16 inches in diameter, with small coils about 2 inches in diameter and 4 inches long at the ends of the diameter. Two copper wires connected the coils to terminals and to a center object about 1 inch in diameter and 2 inches long, likened to a fluorescent-light starter. The center bore the words “MADE IN USA,” and the object reportedly made a sound like a policeman’s whistle. The underside was described as the smooth side facing earth in flight.

**Investigation:** Barksdale Field personnel reportedly took custody of the disc before an FBI Special Agent arrived, and they were making photographs. The message says Barksdale would turn the item over to the FBI if desired, subject to superior instructions, and that the names of all persons who handled it before the agent’s arrival were secured. The report strongly suggests a recovered man-made device or component rather than an unidentified aerial craft, but the document does not record a final technical identification.

**Document:** FBI Communications Section teletype, Washington from Boston 3, dated Jul. 18, 1947, in file 62-HQ-83894. The page is marked “Security Matter-X” and records a post-incident inquiry rather than a direct field report. It is stamped as page one, with “End page one” at the bottom; no continuation page was provided in this extract.

**Witness:** Dean John M. Bunker, security officer at M.I.T., Cambridge, informed the FBI that he had spoken with Charles N. Tasker of West Rindge, New Hampshire, a retired vice president of the New England Telephone and Telegraph Company. Tasker was the relaying source for the original observation made by several unnamed people seated on a porch near the scene.

**Sighting:** Around 3:00 PM on July 7, 1947, observers on a porch saw little curls of smoke on the lawn of Earl Whitehead, Route 2, West Rindge. On inspection, they found small burned spots about 1.5 inches in diameter on the green lawn and additional small blazes in long, dry grass on both sides of the road, within a roughly 200-foot-diameter area. The fire department was called.

**Object/Material:** The fires were reportedly caused by “metallic fragmentations” turned over to Professor Rentges of M.I.T. by Parke D. Appel of the telephone company. Rentges told Bunker the fragments’ general appearance resembled the lining of V-2 bombs he had seen in New Mexico. Another M.I.T. metallurgist, Professor L.H. Newald, suggested they might be from a jet turbo plane. He was analyzing two pieces at the time of the report. The scientists’ rough reconstruction indicated a metallic object approximately 14 inches in diameter. The page does not identify a flying disc, but instead describes debris analysis and possible mundane military/aircraft origins.

001_1947-07-15_Seattle, Washington (2608.report_summary:
**Document:** FBI Seattle sent an urgent teletype to the Director, Communications Section, dated Jul. 16, 1947 at 10:15 AM, under the broader UFO/flying-disc file. The report is a field-originated summary rather than a formal investigative memo, and it records immediate Bureau response and follow-up examination.

**Witness:** Mrs. T. L. Kremmer, identified with an address at 2608 Third Ave. West, Seattle, reported the incident to authorities. The page does not provide a long biographical profile, but her position at the location and the prompt FBI response suggest she was an on-scene civilian observer/occupant rather than a distant hearsay source.

**Sighting:** She said that about 9:42 PM the previous night, a “flying disk” had landed on the roof near her offices and was burning when noticed; it was immediately extinguished. The wording is messy in places, but the core report is of a small object found on/near the roof of the office building, not a distant aerial sighting.

**Object:** Agents were dispatched immediately and recovered the item. Navy bomb and electronics experts, along with FBI agents, examined it. The object was described as a roughly 28-inch circular piece of 3/16-inch plywood cupped on two sides and held by wire across its center, painted light gray outside and red inside. Inside were white-painted markings reading “U S S R” and “E Y R” (apparently “RYE” backward), plus a hammer and sickle. It also contained two radio tubes, an oil can, rubber tubing, a one-inch pipe, and a cloth plug with charred ends.

**Investigation / conclusion:** The physical description strongly suggests a crude homemade or planted device rather than an aircraft or unknown vehicle. The report shows the FBI taking the event seriously enough to dispatch agents and technical experts, but the recovered item’s construction is consistent with a hoax, propaganda device, or odd mechanical assemblage rather than a genuine flying disk.
001_1947-07-15_Seattle, Washington (2608.report_summary_zh:
**Document:** FBI西雅图（Seattle）于1947年7月16日上午10:15向通信处处长发出一份紧急电报，归入更广泛的UFO/飞碟档案之下。该报告更像是一份现场来源的概要，而非正式调查备忘录，并记录了联邦调查局的即时响应及后续检查。

**Witness:** T. L. Kremmer夫人，登记地址为2608 Third Ave. West, Seattle，向当局报告了这一事件。页面未提供详细的个人背景资料，但她所在位置以及FBI的迅速反应表明，她是一名在现场的平民目击者/占有人，而非远距离的转述消息来源。

**Sighting:** 她称在前一晚约9:42 PM，一块“飞碟”落在她办公室附近的屋顶上，被发现时正在燃烧；随即被扑灭。措辞在某些地方较为混乱，但核心内容是：在办公楼屋顶上或附近发现了一件小物体，而非远距离的空中目击。

**Object:** 特工随后立即赶到并将该物体回收。海军炸弹与电子专家连同FBI探员对其进行了检查。该物体被描述为一块约28英寸的圆形3/16英寸胶合板，两侧呈凹形，中央以铁丝固定，外部涂浅灰色、内部涂红色。内部有白漆字样“U S S R”和“E Y R”（显然是“RYE”的倒写），以及一把锤子和镰刀。它还包含两只无线电管、一个油罐、橡胶管、一段一英寸管道，以及一只烧焦两端的布塞。

**Investigation / conclusion:** 其物理特征强烈表明这更像是一个粗糙的自制装置或被人为放置的装置，而不是飞机或未知飞行器。该报告显示FBI对此事相当重视，因而派出了探员和技术专家，但回收物的结构与一场恶作剧、宣传装置或奇特机械拼装物相符，而不像真正的飞碟。

001_1947-06-21_Maury Island (Puget Sound.report_summary:
**Document:** FBI Seattle teletype to the Director in case file 62-HQ-83894, Section 1, dated **AUG 14 1947, 5:15 PM**, marked “ROUTINE” and signed/initialed “WILCOX.” The message is a short intelligence-style follow-up on the Tacoma-area “flying discs” story and notes that the complete report was still en route to Bureau HQ. The page carries standard FBI communications-section stamping and later indexing/recording marks.

**Witness:** The report concerns **Harold A. Dahl** and **Fred Chrisman**, both treated here as civilian witnesses. The Seattle office relays that Dahl did not directly tell “Smith” the story was a hoax, but said that if authorities questioned him he would describe it as a hoax because he wanted no further trouble. That statement, plus the surrounding context, is used by the Bureau to question the credibility of the account.

**Sighting:** The teletype summarizes a “flying discs” sighting in the **Tacoma / Puget Sound area** associated with Chrisman and Dahl. The page itself does not give the full narrative of the observation, but it clearly identifies the incident as the one later known as the Maury Island story. The underlying sighting date is taken as **21 Jun 1947**.

**Object:** The objects are described only generically as “flying discs.” No dimensions, color, number, maneuvering details, or flight path are provided on this page.

**Investigation:** FBI Seattle concludes the anonymous phone call was probably made by Chrisman or Dahl in an effort to build publicity and possibly secure a profitable deal with **Fantasy Magazine, Chicago, Illinois**. The teletype says Dahl and Chrisman would not be reinterviewed unless the Bureau advised otherwise, indicating the Bureau viewed the matter skeptically and suspected a hoax/publicity scheme rather than a reliable UFO report.
001_1947-06-21_Maury Island (Puget Sound.report_summary_zh:

**Object:** 这些物体仅被笼统描述为“flying discs（飞碟）”。本页未提供尺寸、颜色、数量、机动细节或飞行轨迹。

001_1947-08-03_Hackensack, Bergen County.report_summary:
**Document:** Single-page FBI teletype in file **62-HQ-83894, Section 1**. Header reads **“WASHINGTON 1 FROM NEWARK”** and is dated **AUG. 4, 1947, 5:36 PM EDST**; the page is marked **“DIRECTOR URGENT”** and signed/initialed **McKee**. It is a Communications Section transmission reporting a UFO-related sighting and noting that inquiry was underway. No later page in the provided sequence appears to continue this same incident.

**Witness:** The report names **Charles Casella, Jr.**, age 20, of **28 Euclid Avenue, Hackensack**, as the principal observer. It also identifies **William Truex, U.S. Army, Ft. Dix, NJ** as another person who saw the object from the ground on the same occasion. Casella is described as having telephoned the information to the Hackensack Police Department.

**Sighting:** The event is dated to the **late afternoon of August 3, 1947** in **Hackensack, New Jersey**. The object was described as a **“flying disc”** seen from the ground and reportedly at about **200 yards** distance. Casella said it was **in the air**, **revolving slowly**, and **moving rapidly**, and emphasized that it was **neither a kite nor a balloon**. The teletype does not record duration, altitude estimate beyond the 200-yard figure, weather, or any physical effects.

**Investigation:** FBI Newark forwarded the report to FBI headquarters as urgent miscellaneous information. The page states only that **inquiry [was] being made** and that the **Bureau will be kept advised**. No identification or explanation is reached on this page. As a contemporaneous law-enforcement relay of a civilian sighting, the file preserves a first-hand claim but provides no corroborating evidence, making it an unverified visual report rather than a solved case.

001_1947-07-05_Rural Germany (approx. 12.report_summary:
**Document:** Typewritten civilian letter in FBI case file 62-HQ-83894, Section 1 (p. 0147), addressed to the FBI and signed by Robert J. Sroka of 469 N. Washington Ave., Waukesha, Wisconsin. The page bears FBI handling marks/stamps but no separate investigative report or follow-up on this page.

**Witness:** Sroka writes as a former serviceman describing an incident that occurred in Germany "after the war." He says he and a buddy were on pass visiting a friend when the event happened. He offers to swear to the authenticity of what he saw and to the object’s shape, but the letter does not provide a precise incident date.

**Sighting:** While driving on back roads, Sroka spotted a strange object about 8 to 10 miles ahead and roughly 5,000 feet high. He stopped the jeep for a better look. The object then came toward them rapidly while descending slowly. At about a mile away it halted its horizontal motion, continued a slow oscillating descent "similar to a descending parachute," then suddenly dropped in a spiral motion. He drove to the drop point, searched the area for about 10 minutes, and found nothing before darkness forced them to leave.

**Object:** Sroka’s first impression was that it was a cloud, but he notes it moved at right angles to the wind. He characterizes it as disc-shaped in the context of his letter, though the narrative itself emphasizes a hovering/descending object with no landed wreckage or recovered material.

**Investigation:** No official FBI analysis appears on this page; it is an unsolicited sighting report tied to the broader 1947 flying-disc correspondence. The location is given only relative to an apparent place name rendered in the letter as "Habberbishopsheim." The account is single-witness, with uncertain corroboration because Sroka says his companions may have missed the sighting.
001_1947-07-05_Rural Germany (approx. 12.report_summary_zh:

**Witness:** Sroka以一名前军人的身份写信，描述了一起发生在Germany（德国）“战争结束后”的事件。他说，当事件发生时，他和一位伙伴正在休假，去探望一位朋友。他表示愿意为自己所见之事以及该物体的形状宣誓作证，但这封信并未提供确切的事件日期。

**Sighting:** 在乡间小路上驾驶时，Sroka发现前方约8 to 10 miles、约5,000 feet高处有一个奇怪的物体。他停下吉普车仔细观察。随后，该物体迅速朝他们飞来，同时缓慢下降。距离约一mile时，它停止了水平移动，继续以缓慢的摆动式下降，“类似于正在下降的降落伞”，随后突然以螺旋运动向下坠落。他开车赶到坠落点，在该区域搜寻了约10 minutes，未发现任何东西，直到天黑迫使他们离开。

001_1947-08-06_Myrtle Creek, Douglas Cou.report_summary:

**Witness:** The report concerns Red Hatfield, described as a former Navy pilot and the present airport manager at Myrtle Creek, Oregon. His aviation background makes him a comparatively credible observer for the Bureau’s purposes, at least enough to merit prompt follow-up. The teletype states that Hatfield was “to be interviewed.”

**Sighting:** Hatfield reported seeing “a mysterious object” on two occasions on the evening of August 6, 1947, while he was flying at approximately 5,000 feet above Myrtle Creek. The document does not preserve a detailed description of the object’s shape, color, speed, sound, maneuvers, or duration, only that it was viewed twice during the same evening flight.

**Investigation:** The FBI message is an initial field report rather than a completed interview summary. It records the Portland office passing the information to Headquarters for attention under the Bureau’s flying-disc investigation. Because this page is a stand-alone teletype with no continuation page present, the event scope is limited to Hatfield’s reported August 6 sightings over Myrtle Creek and the Bureau’s intent to interview him.

001_1947-07-08_Norfolk, Virginia, USA (4.report_summary:
**Document:** Newspaper clipping from the *Norfolk Ledger-Dispatch* pasted into FBI file 62-HQ-83894, Section 1. The page is stamped dated 7-9-47 and presents a feature story on a photographed “flying disc” in Norfolk. No FBI narrative report, routing sheet, or follow-up memorandum appears on this page.

**Witness:** Bill Turrentine, age 15, of 410 West Fourteenth Street, Norfolk, Virginia. The article says reporter George Hebert interviewed him after he brought in a photograph of the object. Turrentine is portrayed as a local schoolboy who had just returned from summer classes at Maury and was familiar with the “flying saucer” talk then circulating in Norfolk.

**Sighting:** Turrentine said that shortly before noon on Tuesday, 8 July 1947, he stood on the front porch of his home and saw a large gray object moving from the southwest toward the northeast. He described it as “rocking and spinning like a football,” roughly oval rather than disc-shaped, and estimated it was about 5,000 feet high and traveling about 600 mph. He said it appeared to be followed by two smaller objects a few seconds later. He reported no sound.

**Object:** In the article the object is described as “gray, almost black,” with glittering edges and a look “like a burned crisp,” or possibly a rock or stone. Turrentine said it did not resemble a saucer to him, but rather a football. He claimed to have taken three exposures with an old camera set at 1/100 second; one negative produced a usable enlargement.

**Investigation:** The newspaper notes that no other person reported seeing the photographed object. Photo Craftsmen experts were quoted as saying the boy did a good job with the camera and that the film limitation may have reduced detail. The page contains no independent verification, no military assessment, and no analytical conclusion beyond the newspaper’s account.
001_1947-07-08_Norfolk, Virginia, USA (4.report_summary_zh:
**Document:** 《诺福克信使-快报》（Norfolk Ledger-Dispatch）的一则报纸剪报，被粘贴到 FBI 档案 62-HQ-83894 第 1 节中。该页盖有 7-9-47 的日期戳，内容是一篇关于在 Norfolk 拍摄到“飞碟”的特写报道。该页上没有 FBI 的叙述报告、传递单或后续备忘录。

**Witness:** Bill Turrentine，15 岁，住址为 Virginia 州 Norfolk 市 West Fourteenth Street 410 号。文章称，记者 George Hebert 在他带来一张该物体的照片后采访了他。Turrentine 被描绘成当地一名学生，刚从 Maury 的暑期课程回来，并且熟悉当时在 Norfolk 流传的“飞碟”说法。

**Sighting:** Turrentine 说，1947 年 7 月 8 日星期二中午前不久，他站在自家前廊，看到一个巨大的灰色物体从西南方向向东北方向移动。他形容它“像橄榄球一样摇晃并旋转”，外形大致呈椭圆而非圆盘状，并估计它约在 5,000 英尺高空，以大约 600 mph 的速度飞行。他说，几秒钟后，似乎又有两个较小的物体跟随其后。他表示没有听到任何声音。

001_1947-08-08_Norfolk, Virginia (Tidewa.report_summary:
**Document:** FBI letter to the Director, “Re: FLYING DISCS,” dated August 8, 1947. The page shown is the surviving page 2 of the communication (file code 62-182; initialed TJC:lab). It summarizes a prior interview concerning a newspaper-clipped photograph of a flying-disc report from Virginia’s Tidewater area. The letter says Army authorities in the Tidewater Area of Virginia were already aware of the information, so this FBI office would conduct no further investigation.

**Witness:** “Billy,” a local civilian witness and photographer (full surname not legible on this page). He is described as the person who took the picture and later explained the circumstances of the photo to investigators.

**Sighting:** Billy said it took him about 20 to 30 seconds to get the shot. By then the discs were almost directly over his apartment, requiring him to stoop and look nearly perpendicular upward to photograph them. That steep camera angle is cited as the reason a porch railing appears in the newspaper clipping. He added that the weather was hazy and somewhat cloudy.

**Object:** The report refers to “discs” and a “black image” photographed moving from southwest toward northeast, aided by a slight breeze in that same direction. No size, altitude, sound, or maneuvering details are given here, and the page does not report any recovery, identification, or corroborating evidence.

**Assessment:** This is a brief documentary account rather than a full field investigation. The FBI narrative preserves the witness’s explanation of how the photograph was taken, but it reaches no analytic conclusion beyond forwarding the matter and then closing local inquiry once the Army was informed.

The press explanation given was lightning at Campbell River, about 200 miles away, but the clipping frames the dimming as a classic UFO-associated electrical anomaly. Lanuza, Montevideo daylight sightings, and Adamski-related material; those are not part of this incident.

The FBI file page preserves the newspaper account rather than an independent FBI conclusion.

001_1963-12-07_Moorestown, New Jersey, U.report_summary:
**Document:** Typed letter dated March 19, 1969, addressed to FBI Director John Edgar Hoover and preserved in FBI case file 62-HQ-83894, Section 10. The page shows internal routing stamps and handwritten annotations, indicating it was handled as file correspondence rather than a field report.

**Witness:** The writer does not sign his name on this page, but presents himself as a direct observer. He says he made a tape recording of what he saw and previously sent it to J. Edgar Hoover.

**Sighting:** He states that on December 7, 1963, while in the sky at Moorestown, New Jersey, he observed “an unusual object and its unusual behavior.” No time of day is given. The report is retrospective, written more than five years later.

**Object/claim:** The correspondent argues that the object was not an ordinary aircraft or meteorological phenomenon, but “laying air mines.” He claims that this same type of object was connected to the destruction of Pan American World Airways Boeing 707-121 N709PA near Elkton, Maryland, on December 8, 1963, where 73 passengers and 8 crew died. He notes that the Civil Aeronautics Board later issued a March 1965 report attributing the crash to lightning, but says that explanation was wrong and that the investigators “missed the point completely.”

**Investigation:** The writer says he protested to Senator Case of New Jersey, who sent him the official CAB report and a letter from John Dregge (Director, Community and Congressional Relations). He also cites report file #1-0015, page 8, lines 20–24, as supporting his interpretation. The page contains no corroborating analysis; it is a subjective allegation tying a claimed UFO-like observation to an airline disaster.

001_1967-10-09_Dallas, Texas (Dallas FBI.report_summary:
**Document:** FBI Dallas memorandum on U.S. Department of Justice/Federal Bureau of Investigation letterhead, dated October 10, 1967, file reference 62-HQ-83894 (Section 10). The subject line reads “Unidentified Flying Objects; Anonymous Informant; Dallas, Texas; October 9, 1967.” The page includes the standard FBI disclaimer that it contains no recommendations or conclusions and is loaned to another agency.

**Witness:** A young white female, who refused to give her name, appeared at the Dallas FBI Office on October 9, 1967. She said she was interested in UFOs and had received a quantity of information about beings from outer space. She would not reveal her identity, saying she would feel foolish if the information proved untrue, but said she would cooperate further if officials were interested and could ensure her safety.

**Sighting / Claim:** This was not a direct visual sighting report by the witness; it was an anonymous tip containing alleged extraterrestrial contact and second-hand “messages.” She claimed that in July 1967 she met a being from another planet who had assumed earthly form, gave her information, was later “picked up,” and departed Earth on August 21, 1967. She then reportedly received further messages from non-earthly sources, which she would not discuss.

**Object / Allegations:** The information passed to the FBI included four claims: an antimissile missile fired at a UFO over Africa on May 22, 1962, but the craft was protected by a “force field”; a UFO detected 22,000 miles from Earth by radar about August 6, 1967; a UFO detected over Antarctica on August 20, 1967; and a UFO detected over the “Dewline” in the previous week, shot down, with beings from outer space trying to recover it. No corroborating evidence, names, or technical details were provided.

**Investigation:** The memorandum records the informant’s statements only; it does not describe any FBI validation, recommendation, or conclusion. The file is best understood as an intake/reporting document, not an authenticated UFO incident.

001_1973-03-09_Waco, Texas (Waco Tribune.report_summary:
**Document:** These three rendered pages are duplicate/copy views of the same FBI memorandum from San Antonio, Texas, dated March 20, 1973, in FBI file 62-HQ-83894, Section 10. The page text is an internal information report, with the standard FBI notice that it contains no recommendations or conclusions. The first rendered copy also shows handwritten file-control markings and an enclosure stamp, but the underlying narrative is the same across all three pages.

**Witness:** The source named in the memo is Sergeant Paul Stigliano of the United States Air Force Recruiting Office in Waco. He reported what he had been told by the night-shift supervisor at the Waco Tribune Newspaper. The subject of the inquiry was a man identifying himself as Dave T. Ozanne, who claimed to be a U.S. Air Force captain.

**Event:** On March 9, 1973, Ozanne contacted the newspaper supervisor and asked for any information the paper could provide about unidentified flying objects observed in the Waco, Texas area. He was described as wearing an Air Force uniform with a chaplain’s badge and carrying a folder marked “Top Secret” containing photos of various military installations. After being told no information was available, he left a business card listing 3911 Bowser, Apartment 209, Dallas, Texas, phone 526-5908.

**Assessment:** Stigliano stated Ozanne did not behave in a strange manner and made no attempt to obtain anything beyond newspaper information. The memo says the matter was passed to the proper authorities only for information purposes, and that no unlawful activity was suspected. This report does not describe an actual UFO sighting; it documents a suspicious but non-hostile inquiry by a man claiming military credentials.

**Witness:** 备忘录中提到的信息来源是驻沃科（Waco）美国空军招募办公室的保罗·斯蒂格利亚诺（Paul Stigliano）中士。他转述了《Waco Tribune》报纸夜班主管所告诉他的情况。该询问的对象是一名自称戴夫·T·奥扎内（Dave T. Ozanne）的人，他声称自己是一名美国空军上尉。

001_1974-08-21_Milwaukee, Wisconsin (rec.report_summary:
**Document:** FBI Headquarters memorandum on Optional Form No. 10, from T. J. Smith to W. R. Wannall, dated 8/22/74, under file 62-HQ-83894 / REC-101, subject “Military inquiry regarding unidentified object that fell from sky at Milwaukee, Wisconsin, 8/21/74; information concerning.” The page shows routing and initials from FBI offices and staff, indicating internal distribution rather than a field interview report.

**Incident:** At 12:07 a.m. on 8/22/74, Security Patrol Clerk Charles F. Halty of the FBI Intelligence Division received a call through the Command Center from Maj. Horn of NMMC (National Military Command Center). Horn asked whether the FBI had information on a report that an unidentified object had fallen from the sky at Milwaukee and had been recovered by local police and turned over to the Milwaukee FBI Office. A later call to Night Duty Supervisor Harry E. Morris, Jr., confirmed that Milwaukee police had recovered the object at about 5:55 p.m. on 8/21/74 and still possessed it. Capt. Wills of the Milwaukee Police Department had reportedly called the Milwaukee FBI Office about the recovery.

**Object:** The object was described only as about 13 x 8 x 5 inches, metallic in substance and color, jagged on one side, and having an “internal heat source.” No direct eyewitness to the fall is identified in this memo, and the FBI states that very little was known about the object. Police notified military authorities locally.

**Investigation:** The information was relayed back to Maj. Horn with the suggestion that he contact Capt. Wills. The memo notes that the matter received United Press International coverage the morning of 8/22/74. The FBI action was simply “For information,” with no analytical conclusion beyond the limited descriptive facts and the fact of recovery by police.

001_1949-07-01_Lake of the Woods (vicini.report_summary:
**Document:** FBI Office Memorandum, Standard Form No. 64, dated September 6, 1949, from SAC Indianapolis to the Director, FBI, subject “Flying Saucers / Security Matter - X.” The page bears recorded/indexed stamps for file 62-HQ-83894 and is presented as information only; the memo ends by saying the Bureau is taking no action.

**Witness / source chain:** The memo was written after Elbert W. Farris of the OSI at Benjamin Harrison Air Base contacted the Indianapolis FBI office seeking current information on “flying saucers.” Farris said he had been directed to contact Dr. Richard K. Parrish of Decatur, Indiana, who allegedly observed a saucer. The report also mentions an FBI Agent Metcalf of the Omaha office, who was said to have seen the same object.

**Sighting:** Parrish’s alleged observation is placed in the vicinity of Lake of the Woods, Canada, on or about July 1, 1949. The memo does not give a precise time, altitude, direction, size, lights, sound, or flight behavior; the object is referred to only generically as a “flying saucer.”

**Object / interpretation:** The page focuses less on the craft itself than on Parrish’s later interpretation. Farris reported that Parrish believed some Decatur, Indiana polio cases were not polio but possibly uranium poisoning, and that the presence of flying saucers had a bearing on the epidemic. Parrish also cited earlier saucer sightings in the Carolinas in 1948 alongside a polio outbreak there.

**Investigation / disposition:** Farris said he had consulted a physician at Benjamin Harrison Air Base, checked records concerning saucer allegations, and had done research on any correlation between saucer reports and polio outbreaks. He also said he was reporting the matter to Air Force authorities at Wright Field. The memo further notes that Indiana University Medical School personnel treated the matter as a joke. The FBI forwarded the information for Bureau awareness only and did not open action on the matter.

001_1947-08-01_Mountains near Los Angele.report_summary:
**Document:** FBI Headquarters routine telegram in case file **62-HQ-83894, Section 5** (page stamp and routing marks include CC-150, “RECORDED-59 / INDEXED-59,” and Hoover’s signature block). Dated **July 12, 1949**, it was sent to **SAC, Los Angeles** via the Communications Section and directed local agents to discreetly check the subject’s background and interview him for more facts. The memo says the information came from a letter addressed to **Walter Winchell** at a Los Angeles address on West 37th Street.

**Witness:** The report identifies the witness only as **Jones**. No first name, rank, or occupation is given; he appears to be a civilian correspondent whose statement had not yet been independently verified by the FBI.

**Sighting:** Jones wrote that in **August 1947** he was hiking in the mountains out of Los Angeles when he saw, about half a block away, a **large silver metallic object** “shaped like a child’s top” and about the size of a balloon. He said he had the impression that something living was inside it, though he saw no occupant.

**Object/behavior:** When Jones stood up and waved toward the object, it allegedly **took off within a second** and **knocked him to the ground**. The memo gives no corroborating witnesses, no exact date, and no precise mountain location.

**Investigation:** The FBI treated the matter as an unconfirmed lead derived from correspondence rather than a finalized incident report. The Los Angeles office was asked to verify Jones’s background and obtain a direct interview to determine what factual basis, if any, supported the statement.

001_1949-05-27_near Burns, Oregon (Harne.report_summary:
**Document:** Confidential intelligence report DIO-11ND Serial 32-49, issued by the Intelligence Division, Office of Chief of Naval Operations, Navy Department, dated 23 June 1949, preserved in FBI case file 62-HQ-83894 Section 5. Page 1 is a cover sheet with source biography; page 2 contains the narrative report titled "Unidentified Flying Objects Observed in Oregon 27 May 1949."

**Witness:** The source is identified as Joseph C. Shell, USNR (Inactive), a former naval aviator, commercial pilot, flight instructor, and vice-president of the Royal Petroleum Company of California. The report notes a Naval Aviator Certificate, multiple pilot/instructor ratings, and roughly 5,300 total flight hours, which the writer treats as supporting his reliability as an observer.

**Sighting:** On 27 May 1949, about 2:25 p.m. PST, Shell was flying his own SNJ-type aircraft toward Burns, Oregon. He first noticed sunlight glinting off an object ahead and to his left, then realized it was not one object but about six or seven separate objects. The report places the observation over the southern Oregon area near Burns, including the Harney Mountain / dry-lake region, while the objects moved roughly parallel to his course.

**Object:** Shell described the objects as solid, elongated ovals or egg-shaped forms, apparently smaller than a fighter and probably under 20 feet long. He reported no visible wings, fuselage break, exhaust, smoke, or other trail; the objects appeared to be metallic and unpainted. He estimated they were several miles away, 2,000-2,500 feet below his altitude, and moving at roughly 190-260 mph, likely above 230 mph.

**Investigation:** The report relies on a single, technically qualified witness and gives no corroborating observers. The Navy intelligence author did not identify the objects as conventional aircraft and left them classified as unidentified flying objects.

**Sighting:** 1949年5月27日 约下午 2:25（PST），Shell 正驾驶其自有的 SNJ 型飞机飞往俄勒冈州 Burns。起初，他注意到前方左侧有一物体反射阳光；随后才意识到那并非单一物体，而是大约六七个彼此分离的物体。报告将此次目击地点置于俄勒冈州南部 Burns 附近地区，包括 Harney Mountain / 干湖（dry-lake）一带，而这些物体大致沿着他的飞行航向平行移动。

**Document:** Confidential DIO-11MD Serial 39-49, subject "Unidentified Flying Objects - Report Of," dated 23 June 1949. This single page appears to be the complete report extract available here; no follow-on pages are included in the provided sequence. The page contains an intelligence-style evaluation and coordinate reconstruction rather than a newspaper clipping or later summary.

**Witness:** The observer is identified only as "Source" and is described as an expert pilot-instructor. The page gives the source's aircraft position when the objects left visual range as about 42°41'N, 119°49'W, and notes that his track was flown in a straight line between the plotted coordinates. The narrative suggests the source was airborne and experienced enough to estimate positions and bearings with some confidence.

**Sighting:** The report places the objects first at approximately 42°38'N, 119°43'W and last at approximately 42°28'N, 119°48'W, over the south-central Oregon high desert. The text says the source's plotted position could have been as much as five miles SSW of the stated point, indicating the locations are approximate and derived from the source's reconstruction of the encounter. The page does not preserve a precise sighting clock time in the visible text.

**Object:** The objects are described only generically as "unidentified flying objects"/"strange flying objects," with the discussion focused on their observed positions and the source's visual range rather than on color, shape, or formation details in the visible excerpt.

**Investigation:** The reporting officer concludes that conventional aircraft, balloons, astronomical phenomena, and autokinesis can be eliminated as explanations. The memo leaves the cause unresolved, noting that the source's comments and the officer's analysis do not provide a satisfactory identification. The report's provenance and language indicate an internal military-intelligence evaluation, later preserved in the FBI case file.

001_1949-09-25_Lubeck area, west of Sout.report_summary:
**Document:** These three consecutive pages form one FBI/UFO correspondence chain around the same sighting. Page 0039 is a Standard Form 64 office memorandum from the SAC, Pittsburgh to the Director, FBI, dated October 2, 1949, forwarding the attached letter from Glen Sprouse. Page 0040 is Sprouse’s original letter to the FBI, dated September 25, 1949. Page 0041 is a Headquarters memorandum from J. Edgar Hoover to the Air Force Inspector General, dated October 19, 1949, summarizing the same report as unverified information from a confidential source. File markings include 62-HQ-83894-202 and exhibit tags EX-119/EX-119A.

**Witness:** Glen Sprouse of 608 Montrose Drive, S. Charleston, West Virginia, reported the event after voluntarily appearing at the Charleston resident agency and turning over his letter to Special Agent John B. Woodruff. He stated he was the pilot of a Luscombe 8A (NC 1440K) and was flying with his wife, who did not see the object.

**Sighting:** On September 25, 1949, at about 2:45 P.M., while flying from Clark Field, St. Albans, to Parkersburg, Sprouse said that roughly four miles southwest of Parkersburg, over a dark green wooded background, he suddenly saw a bright yellow object moving directly toward him. It passed in a few seconds about 100 feet below his aircraft and about 50 feet to the right.

**Object:** Sprouse described a bright canary-yellow body, about 15 to 18 inches long and roughly 4 inches in diameter at its widest point. He said it looked like a rocket, with the same general proportions as the fuselage of a Lockheed Air Force X-90, but with no wings and with vertical and horizontal fins near the rear third. He reported a very sharp needle nose, a blunt tail, and no visible propulsion, smoke, vapor trail, or exhaust. He believed it was not a mirage and said it appeared to be dropping slightly as it passed.

**Investigation:** The FBI recorded the report but took no further action unless directed. Hoover’s later memo repeated that the information was unverified and came from a source whose reliability was unknown. The file preserves the sighting as a daylight, close-range, pilot-observed UFO report, but no identification or explanation was reached.

001_1950-03-09_Denver University (Denver.report_summary:
**Document:** FBI Denver sent an urgent teletype to the Director, FBI, at 9:25 PM on 9 Mar 1950 in case file 62-HQ-83894, Section 5. The page is marked with internal routing/approval initials and signed "Kramer." It reads like an intelligence lead rather than a formal field report.

**Witness:** No direct eyewitness is named. The report says two sources advised the Bureau that an unidentified man had given at least one, and possibly more, lectures before classes at Denver University. The man reportedly refused to reveal his identity, but was known to George Koehler, who was connected with radio station KMYR, Denver.

**Sighting:** The lecturer allegedly said he had personally observed flying saucers. He claimed to have seen several such objects, one of which allegedly landed in New Mexico. He also claimed to have observed occupants of the saucers, describing them as human in form but about three feet tall, and said these occupants were dead when he saw them.

**Investigation:** The FBI note says local press and wire services were already carrying stories about the Denver University lectures. OSI Denver reported no additional information, except that Koehler had made similar claims in January and, after investigation, had been unable to produce verifiable information. OSI considered Koehler a probable mental case. The page contains no corroborated physical evidence and no confirmed identity for the lecturer; it is best read as a report of sensational UFO claims circulating through local media and informants, not as a validated sighting.

**Investigation:** The page is best treated as an uncorroborated citizen data submission asking the FBI to compare the dates with other saucer reports. No follow-up finding, witness interview, or Project Saucer/Air Force conclusion appears on this page.

001_1950-03-22_New Mexico, USA (reported.report_summary:
**Document:** Single-page FBI Office Memorandum (Standard Form No. 64) in case file **62-HQ-83894**, Section 5, from **Guy Hottel, SAC, Washington**, to the Director, FBI, dated **March 22, 1950**. The page is stamped/annotated for FBI record control and marked **RECORDED** and **INDEXED** on **Mar 29, 1950**. Subject line: **“Flying Saucers – Information Concerning.”**

**Source chain:** Hottel states that the information was furnished to **SA R. H. Kurtzman** by **Karl Howe**, identified as a **Special Investigator, Sex Squad, Metropolitan Police Department**. The memo does not name the original Air Force investigator; the account is entirely secondhand and uncorroborated.

**Sighting / claim:** Howe’s informant allegedly said that **three “flying saucers”** had been recovered in **New Mexico**. They were described as circular craft with raised centers, about **50 feet in diameter**. Each was said to contain **three human-shaped bodies** only **3 feet tall**, dressed in metallic, fine-textured cloth and bandaged in a manner similar to blackout suits used by speed flyers and test pilots. The alleged reason given for the New Mexico recovery was that a **very high-powered radar set-up** in that area interfered with the saucers’ controlling mechanism.

**Assessment:** The memo contains no dates, coordinates, witness first-hand observations, or investigative follow-up. Hottel explicitly notes that **no further evaluation was attempted**. The record reads as an unverified rumor or hearsay report rather than a documented sighting, and its provenance is FBI correspondence rather than an actual field investigation.

**Document:** FBI Buffalo teletype to the Director, FBI, marked **URGENT** in file **62-HQ-83894, Section 5**. The page is dated **4-8-50, 12:52 PM**, with a later routing/record stamp on **Apr 26 1950** and a signed sender line reading **MAYNOR**. A typed correction notes that the fifth line, fourth word should be **“attached”**.

**Witness / source:** The report does not name a civilian witness. It says information came from the **Elmira Police Department**, and that the **resident agent at Elmira** followed up on the complaint. No individual is identified as having observed the object in flight.

001_1949-06-23_Warner Valley, Oregon (Ha.report_summary:
**Document:** FBI memorandum in file 62-HQ-83894, Section 5, serial 58-49, subject line “Unidentified Flying Objects – Report of,” dated 23 June 1949. The page is marked confidential/classified-style and appears to be an analytical summary rather than a first-person narrative. No signer is visible on this page.

**Witness:** The source is an experienced aircraft pilot who regularly flew between California and Oregon. The memo treats him as a credible observer: he knew the valley route, could estimate altitudes, and was familiar with the terrain and traffic patterns. He reported that he had not seen other aircraft in the valley on prior flights and believed the area was sparsely populated but not empty.

**Sighting:** The objects were seen over a north-south valley in south-central Oregon, described as about 12 miles wide with a floor around 4,000–5,000 feet MSL and the east side dominated by Hart Mountain / a dark bluff. The source was flying north while the objects moved south. From an estimated 9,000-foot aircraft altitude, the objects were judged to be roughly in line with the 7,000-foot rim of the bluff and probably around 8,000 feet MSL, or about 3,500 feet above the valley floor. Visibility was said to be exceptionally good, with scattered clouds high overhead and only light haze.

**Object:** At first the witness could not separate the lights/reflections, but as he closed to within about 5–7 miles he distinctly saw 5 to 8 separate objects, probably 6 or 7. They were always in single-file formation with very constant spacing, showing no obvious change in relative altitude. The memo says they appeared metallic or “unpainted metal,” stood out sharply against the dark terrain, and were rigidly grouped; terrain could reportedly be seen between them. The analyst noted the formation’s spacing and motion suggested multiple separate craft rather than a single object.

**Investigation:** The report notes the valley is sparsely populated, with ranches that might yield ground witnesses, but it is not a commercial airline route and is seldom used by private aircraft. The page offers no final identification or explanation.
001_1949-06-23_Warner Valley, Oregon (Ha.report_summary_zh:

**Witness:** 信息来源是一名经验丰富的飞行员，常年往返于 California 和 Oregon 之间飞行。备忘录将其视为可靠目击者：他熟悉山谷航线，能够估算飞行高度，并且熟悉地形和空中交通模式。他报告说，此前飞越该山谷时未见到其他飞机，并认为该地区人口稀少，但并非无人居住。

**Sighting:** 这些物体是在 Oregon 中南部一条南北走向的山谷上空被看到的，该山谷被描述为宽约 12 英里，谷底海拔约 4,000–5,000 feet MSL，东侧以 Hart Mountain / 一处黑色峭壁为主。目击者当时向北飞行，而这些物体则向南移动。根据估计的 9,000-foot 飞机高度，这些物体被判断大致与 7,000-foot 的峭壁边缘齐平，且很可能位于约 8,000 feet MSL，即比谷底高约 3,500 feet。文中称能见度极佳，头顶高空有零散云层，仅有轻微薄雾。

**Document:** FBI Houston teletype(s) to the Director in the Communications Section, file 62-HQ-83894 (Section 5), dated July 4, 1950. The first transmission at 2:35 PM CST reported a “flying disc” said to have been found near Alice, Texas, and noted a reported serial number “X-147A” plus instructions quoted as “do not touch.” A second Houston teletype at 3:50 PM CST follows up with the result of the inquiry.

Initial descriptions characterized it as a small, elliptical contraption about five feet in diameter, freshly painted, and bearing the markings mentioned in the first teletype.

**Investigation:** McEnheimer advised that the object was built by welding together portions of two airplane wings. It had no motor or means of propulsion, and after examination the police concluded it had been constructed by a group of mechanics at the Alice airport as a practical joke. Air Force officials at Ellington Field were notified, and the Bureau closed the matter with no further inquiry. 001_1950-06-27_Louisville, Kentucky (nea.report_summary:

**Sighting:** On **1950-06-27 about 4:15 p.m.**, at **Longest and Everett Avenues near 2205 Longest, Louisville, Kentucky**, Hixenbaugh reported hearing a big plane (described as a **twin-motored DC-3**) overhead, then looking west of the plant and seeing a **large disk**. The object reportedly had a **slight corona**, appeared **lower than the plane**, remained **motionless for about ten seconds**, then **got smaller** and finally **vanished into the west**.

No official conclusion is stated on this page, but the report notes that military officers at **Godman Field** were notified and flight headquarters at **Wright-Patterson Field** were informed. The memo preserves the incident as a contemporaneous press-and-bureau summary of a photographed UFO sighting rather than a completed investigation.

001_1950-01-22_Kodiak Naval Air Station.report_summary:
**Document:** Confidential memo, DIC/17TD No. 4-50, dated 10 February 1950, subject “Unidentified Phenomena.” The page is numbered 2 and summarizes information from enclosures (1) through (8). It appears in FBI case-file material but describes Navy-origin reports from the Kodiak, Alaska area.

**Witnesses:** The primary witness is Lt. L. T. Smith, USN, patrol plane commander of PV/PBY patrol aircraft with Patrol Squadron One. Additional observers include radar operator G. Skeen, USN; Morgan, FTC, USN aboard USS *Tilamook* (ATA-192); Carver, CN, USN; and later Lt. Causer, Lt. Parco, and plane captain Paulson.

**Sighting:** The page describes several related events around Kodiak on 22-23 January 1950. Smith first reported an unidentified radar contact about 20 miles north of NAS Kodiak, then another contact about 10 miles southeast of the station. During the same period he was also involved in a visual/radar encounter in which an object appeared on the radar scope at about 5 miles, then came directly overhead, reportedly suggesting very high speed. He estimated roughly 1,800 mph and said the object maneuvered too quickly for him to intercept or circle.

**Object:** Descriptions vary by observer but include a very fast-moving red light, a “ball of fire” about one foot in diameter, a blip with a tail-like indication on radar, and an airborne object that seemed to open out, turn left, and come up on the aircraft’s quarter. No sound was detected in the shipboard sighting. The object later departed to the southeast. Another patrol the following day reportedly saw an unidentified object on an ascending westerly course for about ten minutes, but could not close with it at 170 knots.

**Assessment:** The report reflects trained military observers, multiple corroborating sightings, and at least some radar involvement, but the page offers no identification or firm conclusion. The observations are brief, inconsistent in appearance, and partly dependent on radar interpretation; the document itself frames them as unexplained phenomena rather than a solved incident.
001_1950-01-22_Kodiak Naval Air Station.report_summary_zh:
**Document:** 机密备忘录，DIC/17TD No. 4-50，日期为 1950年2月10日，主题为“Unidentified Phenomena.”。该页编号为 2，并汇总了附件（1）至（8）中的信息。其出现在 FBI 案卷材料中，但所述内容为来自 Alaska(阿拉斯加) Kodiak(科迪亚克) 地区的海军报告。

**Witnesses:** 主要目击者为 Lt. L. T. Smith, USN，Patrol Squadron One 的 PV/PBY 巡逻机机长。其他观察者包括雷达操作员 G. Skeen, USN；USS *Tilamook* (ATA-192) 舰上的 Morgan, FTC, USN；Carver, CN, USN；以及后来的 Lt. Causer、Lt. Parco 和机长 Paulson。

**Sighting:** 该页描述了 1950年1月22日至23日围绕 Kodiak(科迪亚克) 发生的几起相关事件。Smith 首先报告称，在 NAS Kodiak(科迪亚克海军航空站) 以北约 20 英里处发现一个不明雷达目标，随后又在该站东南约 10 英里处发现另一个目标。在同一期间，他还参与了一次目视/雷达遭遇：一个物体先在约 5 英里处出现在雷达显示器上，随后直接飞越其上空，据称表明其速度极高。他估计速度约为 1,800 mph，并表示该物体机动过快，无法拦截或绕飞。

**Object:** 不同观察者对其描述不尽相同，包括一个高速移动的红色光点、一个直径约一英尺的“火球”、雷达上带有尾迹样指示的回波，以及一个空中物体，看起来会突然展开、左转并向飞机右后方上升靠近。在舰上目击中未探测到任何声音。该物体随后向东南方向离去。次日的另一次巡逻据称在一个上升的向西航向上观察到一个不明物体，持续约十分钟，但在 170 knots 速度下无法追上它。

**Assessment:** 这份报告反映了经过训练的军事观察员、多个相互印证的目击，以及至少一定程度的雷达参与，但该页并未给出任何确认身份或明确结论。所述观察持续时间短、外观描述不一致，且部分依赖雷达解读；文件本身将其定性为无法解释的现象，而非已解决事件。

001_1950-07-19_Toronto, Ontario, Canada.report_summary:
**Document:** Single-page letter on Walter D. Jones letterhead (36 King Street East, Toronto, Ont.) dated **August 29, 1950**, addressed to the **Federal Bureau of Investigation, Washington, D.C.** The page is part of FBI file **62-HQ-83894, Section 5** and is marked with later FBI handling stamps (“Recorded-90,” “Indexed-90”). No continuation or separate report pages are present in the provided sequence.

**Witness:** The author/signatory is **Walter D. Jones**, who states he was observing his farm near Toronto. He writes as a civilian eyewitness and mentions calling over his “houseman” for corroboration. The houseman watched the object for about ten minutes while Jones continued observing it.

**Sighting:** Jones reports that on **July 19 at 10:30 p.m.** he was looking west over his farm. He says the moon was fairly full and there was a low ceiling of light clouds. Through the clouds he saw a **hazy object of light** approaching the farmhouse at **incredible speed**. It circled before reaching the farmhouse and continued circling; Jones says he could not determine its height, orbit, or shape because it was above the clouds and visible only as a “filter of light.” He adds that it sometimes seemed to slow, then circle in the opposite direction.

**Object:** The object is described only as a bright, hazy light with no discernible structure, beam source, or form. Jones estimates total observation time at about **35 minutes** (10:30 p.m. to 11:05 p.m.), with the object disappearing westward.

**Investigation:** Jones states he is passing the information to the FBI “for what it is worth” and suggests discarding it if unwanted. The letter is a straightforward eyewitness report rather than an FBI investigative memorandum. Based on the text alone, the incident remains **unresolved**, with no corroborating measurements, photos, or physical evidence beyond a second witness’s brief observation.

001_1950-09-26_Philadelphia, Pennsylvani.report_summary:
**Document:** FBI Office Memorandum (Standard Form No. 64), dated October 2, 1950, from the SAC, Philadelphia, to the Director, FBI, attention Mr. Leo Laughlin. Subject line: “Flying Disc Reported at Philadelphia on 9/26/50.” The page carries FBI routing and later handling marks, including a note that the matter was referred to Air Force Intelligence and then to OSI, with no further FBI action taken.

**Witness:** The report is based on two Philadelphia police officers on duty, described as observing the incident firsthand in the late evening hours of September 26, 1950. No individual names are given in this memo, so the witness set is limited to their official role and agency.

**Sighting:** While on Vare Boulevard near 26th Street in Philadelphia, the officers saw a round object about six feet in circumference slowly float down to the ground. It reportedly had the appearance of a parachute and came to rest in a field without depressing the weeds, suggesting it was extremely light. The object was described as lavender in color and “dewy,” “sort of like soap suds,” and it evaporated within 15 to 20 minutes after landing. When touched by the officers, the substance disappeared, leaving only a slight sticky residue.

**Assessment / provenance:** The memo states the report was made to the FBI by the Philadelphia Police and later appeared in the Philadelphia press under the headline “Flying Saucer Just Dissolves.” The language of the report strongly suggests a transient foam-like or soap-suds-like material rather than a conventional metallic craft, and the memo records no definitive identification. The FBI treated it as a field report to be passed to Air Force Intelligence, not as an active FBI investigation.

001_1950-10-20_New Haven, Connecticut (b.report_summary:
**Document:** FBI memorandum dated November 24, 1950, from J. Edgar Hoover, Director of the Federal Bureau of Investigation, to the Director of Special Investigations, Office of the Inspector General, Department of the Air Force, Pentagon. The page is marked as an FBI file item in case 62-HQ-83894 (red notation and routing stamps), and it summarizes a field report received by the New Haven FBI office.

**Witness:** Aaron L. 001_1950-06-17_Hasselbach, Thuringia, Ge.report_summary:
**Document:** Page 0178 is a press-clipping page in FBI HQ file 62-HQ-83894, Section 6. The UFO item is a Sunday Graphic article dated July 6, 1952, by Antony Terry from Berlin, headlined “50 Yards Away I Saw Two Men Take Off in a ‘Flying Saucer.’” No FBI investigative memorandum, classification stamp, or Bureau analytical conclusion is visible on this page; it preserves a newspaper account of a sworn statement being reviewed by Western/West Berlin officials.

**Witness:** The principal witness is Oskar Linke, described as a 48-year-old ex-mayor from Gleimershausen near Meiningen who had escaped from the Russian zone with his wife and six children. The article says Linke and his 11-year-old stepdaughter Gabriele gave a solemn affidavit before a judge, increasing the reported evidentiary value of the account.

**Sighting:** Linke stated that on June 17, 1950, while riding a motorcycle with Gabriele as passenger near Hasselbach, a tire problem caused them to stop. In the half-light Gabriele pointed out something roughly 150 yards away. Linke first thought it was a deer, then approached to about 60 yards and eventually to about 30 feet behind a ridge.

**Object:** Linke reported two human-like figures wearing a shimmering metallic substance, bending near a large oval object he compared to a “warming pan.” He estimated it at roughly 40–50 feet across, with rows of holes along the sides and a black cylindrical “conning tower” about 10 feet high. When Gabriele called out, the figures hurried into the object. Linke said the craft emitted changing green-to-red light and a humming sound, the conning tower retracted, and the object rose and departed toward Stockheim.

**Investigation:** The article says other local people later reported seeing what they thought was a comet-like object, and Linke claimed he found a fresh circular depression where the craft had stood. A sidebar quoted Vickers aircraft designer George Edwards as saying the described machine did not resemble known conventional aircraft, though vertical takeoff was conceptually possible. The page presents the case as possible evidence of a secret Soviet “flying saucer,” but contains no FBI finding validating the report.
